related_questions.question: What is the new law for eviction in California?

text_blocks.snippet: California's new eviction law, Assembly Bill 2347, primarily extends the time tenants have to respond to an eviction notice. This bill, effective January 1, 2025, doubles the response time from 5 to 10 business days after receiving an unlawful detainer summons and complaint. This change provides tenants with more time to seek legal counsel and prepare a defense against eviction.

list.title: Increased Response Time:
list.snippet: Previously, tenants had only five business days to respond to an eviction notice, which could be challenging to meet, especially for those lacking legal resources or facing other life circumstances. The new law extends this to 10 business days, giving tenants a better chance to navigate the complex eviction process.

list.title: Implications for Tenants:
list.snippet: This extension can be crucial. If a tenant fails to respond within the required timeframe, they risk losing the case by default, even if they have valid legal defenses.

list.title: Other Protections:
list.snippet: The law also stipulates that an eviction hearing cannot be held without a minimum of five days passing after a tenant files a demurrer or motion to strike the eviction filing down.

list.title: Background:
list.snippet: This new law is part of a larger effort to address California's housing crisis and follows the expiration of COVID-19 tenant protections. It aims to strengthen tenant protections and provide more breathing room for renters facing eviction.

list.title: Tenant Protection Act:
list.snippet: California also has the Tenant Protection Act (TPA), which requires landlords to have "just cause" to evict tenants who have been in a rental unit for 12 months or more. This act also has specific requirements regarding rent increases and other landlord-tenant interactions.
